messages.content: You write the short explanations that first-year programming students in India type when a C quiz asks them "Why did you choose that answer?". Reply with a JSON object only.

A student was shown this C code and question.

Code:
int sum(int a[], int n) { return a[n - 1] + sum(a, n - 1); }
// a = {1, 2, 3}

Question: What is sum(a, 3)?
The student answered: 6

The student holds this wrong belief and does not know it is wrong: Recursion stops by itself when the work is done

Write 5 different explanations this student might type for why they chose that answer.
Voice: long-winded, walks through the steps one by one, 20 to 35 words.

Rules:
- Each one must show the student's reasoning, not just repeat the answer.
- Write as the student, in the first person or with no subject. Do not judge the answer or say it is wrong.
- Do not name the idea as a rule and do not use textbook terms for the mistake.
- Make the 5 explanations differ in wording and in which part of the code they point at.

Return JSON: {"sentences": ["...", "..."]}

content: {"sentences": ["Since a has 1, 2, 3 at positions zero, one, two, calling sum with n as three adds the last item 3 and keeps adding until the list finishes naturally.", "Looking at a[n minus 1] plus sum with n minus 1, the first return grabs a[2] which is 3, then the pattern just continues down the array indexes and totals six.", "The code adds a[2], then a[1], then a[0], and because all the array items get used up the function knows there is nothing left and gives back six automatically.", "Tracing n equals 3, then 2, then 1, each step adds the next value from the array, so 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 6 and the adding stops once every element has been counted.", "Because the function keeps calling sum with smaller n values, it eventually reaches the first array slot, sums 1, 2, and 3 together, and returns six without needing any extra stopping line."]}

sentences: Since a has 1, 2, 3 at positions zero, one, two, calling sum with n as three adds the last item 3 and keeps adding until the list finishes naturally.
Looking at a[n minus 1] plus sum with n minus 1, the first return grabs a[2] which is 3, then the pattern just continues down the array indexes and totals six.
The code adds a[2], then a[1], then a[0], and because all the array items get used up the function knows there is nothing left and gives back six automatically.
Tracing n equals 3, then 2, then 1, each step adds the next value from the array, so 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 6 and the adding stops once every element has been counted.
Because the function keeps calling sum with smaller n values, it eventually reaches the first array slot, sums 1, 2, and 3 together, and returns six without needing any extra stopping line.
